92c37a8def1ad20659b82eba04c2aaec4efc9cca.summary: Fortinet FortiGuard Labs describes a Russian-language phishing email carrying a Zip archive with a decoy PowerPoint file and a macro add-in. The macro drops a VBScript that creates a scheduled task for persistence and tries to reach a command and control server. The report links the activity to the Konni RAT, tied to the group APT 37, which it says aligns with North Korean government objectives. The command and control server was not responding, so the RAT itself was not obtained.

927e005f5cdd9887481a10b2b8a854ec57389e5b.summary: A Malpedia family page for Dridex, a banking Trojan. It is mainly an index of third-party reports and blog posts about Dridex, listed by date, title and author. The short quoted passages describe Dridex as an information-stealing malware that sends credentials over an encrypted tunnel to numerous scattered command-and-control servers, and note that an older macro-based infection method faded after Microsoft Office updates, and that IBM X-Force reported Dridex v4 using AtomBombing code injection. It is a reference index rather than a threat report, so no facts are recorded.

audit_history.note: summary: Reverses the order of events. The text says the attackers move laterally first, and obtaining Domain Admin rights is their 'next objective', not a step

92fa8220e78baab4a4e686370664a5d9071678e4.summary: Palo Alto Networks' Unit 42 describes P2PInfect, a self-replicating peer-to-peer worm written in Rust. It infects Redis instances on Linux and Windows by exploiting CVE-2022-0543 in the Lua sandbox. Unit 42 first found it on July 11, 2023 in its HoneyCloud honeypots. The worm uses a P2P network to distribute follow-up payloads and scanners. Unit 42 found no definitive evidence of cryptomining, but notes that the network's auto-update features could let its operators push more capable payloads. It recommends monitoring Redis instances and updating them.
